name: Keto / ketogenic diet

lead: The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, very low-carbohydrate diet. It was developed as a medical therapy for refractory epilepsy, mainly in children, and is now popular for losing body fat and getting a leaner face and body. Some people also report it calming acne.

With little carbohydrate, the liver makes ketone bodies that replace glucose as fuel, and appetite often drops, so body fat falls. Wikipedia reports low-carbohydrate diets produce somewhat more short-term weight loss than low-fat diets, with the advantage fading over time, and a 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years. Acne effects are not covered in the sources consulted.

paras: People cut most bread, pasta, sugar and starchy foods and build meals around meat, fish, eggs, dairy, oils and low-carb vegetables, often tracking carbs to stay in ketosis. Early weight changes are partly water and show within the first weeks.

Reported effects include constipation, early fatigue, raised lipids and, rarely, ketoacidosis, with case reports documented. People with diabetes, pregnancy or medical conditions are generally advised to consult a clinician first.

angle.text: Very low carbohydrate intake lowers appetite and body fat for a leaner face and body, and some users report calmer skin. Keto is an established epilepsy therapy with mixed weight loss results; acne effects were not covered in the sources here.

lead: The ketogenic (keto) diet is a very low-carbohydrate, high-fat eating pattern with moderate protein, in which the liver produces ketone bodies that serve as fuel in place of glucose.[1][2] It began as a medical therapy for epilepsy and became one of the most searched diets in the United States by 2020.[3] People in fitness and looksmaxxing circles use it to lose body fat and look leaner, which makes the jawline, cheekbones and muscle definition more visible, and some also try it hoping for clearer skin.[4][5]

Short-term trials of low-carbohydrate diets report somewhat greater weight loss than low-fat diets, with the gap narrowing over time. A meta-analysis of randomized trials in overweight adults with type 2 diabetes found larger reductions in body weight and waist circumference on a ketogenic diet,[6] and a 2025 randomized trial compared keto with time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting in adults with obesity.[7] In trained people, small randomized trials report fat loss on keto with mixed results for lean mass: one found fat-mass reductions in a ketogenic group while muscle gain appeared only in a non-ketogenic group, and another in competitive bodybuilders found fat loss alongside similar strength gains.[8][9]

The diet is also tied to a wider online culture: Robert Atkins's 1970s books, Gary Taubes's carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis, and in recent years carnivore and animal-based variants promoted by figures such as Shawn Baker and Paul Saladino.[10][11][12] In forums, keto is discussed as a cutting tool, with members posting leanness checks and weight-loss logs, while others argue that carbohydrates matter for muscle gain.[13][4][14] Clinicians and reviewers report side effects ranging from constipation and early fatigue to raised LDL cholesterol.[1][15]

paras: A classic ketogenic diet derives most calories from fat and restricts carbohydrate to a small amount so the body produces ketones. In the epilepsy setting the classic version uses a 4:1 ratio of fat to combined protein and carbohydrate, with weighed food and vitamin supplements.[1] Nutritional ketosis is generally described as occurring when carbohydrate falls under roughly 50 g a day for several days, though the threshold varies with activity, insulin sensitivity and genetics; blood ketones normally sit below 0.5 mM and stay below about 3 mM in physiological ketosis.[2]

The three ketone bodies are acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate (the main circulating one) and acetone. Ketosis differs from ketoacidosis, an uncontrolled and dangerous acidosis seen mostly with insulin deficiency in diabetes.[2] Ketone status can be checked with urine strips (which detect only acetoacetate), finger-stick blood meters for beta-hydroxybutyrate, or breath tests.[2]

Medical variants include the medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) diet, introduced by Peter Huttenlocher in 1971, the modified Atkins diet first reported in 2003, and the low glycemic index treatment, which allows about 40 to 60 g of carbohydrate a day.[1] Very-low-calorie ketogenic diets are used in research on weight and conditions such as lipedema.[16] Variants discussed in lifting forums include cyclical keto, with a carbohydrate day once a week, and targeted approaches around training.[17] Carnivore and animal-based diets overlap with keto in their low carbohydrate intake and are described below.[12]

Fasting and restricted diets for epilepsy are traced back to the Hippocratic writings, and Hugh Conklin's water diet was widely adopted from 1916.[1] The term ketogenic diet was coined in 1921 by Russell Wilder at the Mayo Clinic, and Mynie Peterman reported in 1925 that 60 percent of 37 children became seizure-free.[1] Use declined after phenytoin arrived in 1938 and again after sodium valproate in the 1970s.[1]

Weight-loss use has a separate lineage. William Banting, an English undertaker, published a widely read letter in 1863 advising against bread, butter, milk, sugar, beer and potatoes, and Robert Atkins published Dr. Atkins' Diet Revolution in 1972, drawing on earlier work by Alfred Pennington.[10] Atkins Nutritionals was founded in 1989; about one in eleven North American adults reported following a low-carbohydrate diet at the peak in 2003, a share that fell to about 2 percent in 2004, and the company filed for Chapter 11 in 2005.[10]

The modern epilepsy revival followed Jim Abrahams's account of his son Charlie's treatment, featured on NBC's Dateline in October 1994, which led to the Charlie Foundation, a multicentre study published in 1998 and the 1997 TV film First Do No Harm.[1] The diet was offered at about 75 centres in 45 countries by 2007.[1] Keto reached mass popularity in the late 2010s, and the global ketogenic food market was valued at about 9.6 billion dollars in 2019.[3]

With little carbohydrate, glycogen stores and blood glucose fall, the liver shifts toward fatty-acid oxidation, and ketones supply the brain and other tissues.[2] Proponents describe this as a metabolic switch that lowers appetite, steadies energy and reduces insulin levels. Gary Taubes popularised the carbohydrate-insulin hypothesis in Good Calories, Bad Calories (2007) and Why We Get Fat (2010), proposing that carbohydrates, especially sugar, overstimulate insulin and promote fat storage.[11] Taubes and Peter Attia founded the Nutrition Science Initiative in 2012 to test it; a 2014 pilot study led by NIH researcher Kevin Hall did not support the hypothesis, according to Wikipedia, and critics such as Harriet Hall dispute Taubes's reading of the literature.[11]

Researchers examining energy balance report different findings. In a metabolic-ward study of 17 overweight or obese men, an isocaloric ketogenic diet produced small increases in energy expenditure, but fat loss slowed during the ketogenic phase and the authors concluded it was not accompanied by increased body fat loss.[18] A review of the insulin and weight-loss literature discusses whether insulin sensitivity improves before or after weight loss.[19] Wikipedia summarises that calorie intake and adherence appear to matter more than macronutrient ratios over the long term.

Proponents say cutting carbohydrate reduces appetite and water retention so they lean out faster, and some users post physique checks while on the diet.[4][14] Wikipedia reports that low-carbohydrate diets give somewhat more short-term loss than low-fat diets, around 100 kcal a day, a gap that fades; a 2022 Cochrane review is described as finding no benefit over balanced diets at two years, and early loss is likely largely water.[10] For looks, the chain is leanness: lower body fat shows more bone structure in the face and more muscle definition.

Several small trials address physique. Among 24 trained men doing eight weeks of resistance training in an energy surplus, only the ketogenic group lost fat mass and visceral fat while muscle mass rose only in the non-ketogenic group.[9] In 19 competitive natural bodybuilders randomized for two months, the ketogenic group lost body fat and the Western-diet group gained lean mass, with similar strength gains; the authors suggested keto may suit contest preparation while possibly blunting muscle growth.[8] A trial of 25 young men found a cyclical ketogenic reduction diet and a balanced reduction diet gave similar weight and fat loss, while the ketogenic group lost lean mass and body water and strength and endurance improved only in the balanced group.[20] Wikipedia notes that low-carbohydrate diets have been found to reduce endurance during intense exercise.

Acne is the main skin claim attached to keto. A 2012 review in Skin Pharmacology and Physiology proposed mechanisms by which ketogenic diets might help, such as lower insulin and carbohydrate load, and framed them as proposals rather than demonstrated effects.[21] A 2024 review in Critical Reviews in Food Science and Nutrition described the evidence as sparse and presented the use as speculative,[5] and a 2025 Frontiers in Nutrition review described limited evidence concentrated on acne, psoriasis, hidradenitis suppurativa and melanoma, alongside reported adverse skin effects.[22]

One uncontrolled study followed 31 young women with moderate acne and grade I obesity on a 45-day very-low-calorie ketogenic diet and reported significant falls in acne severity and quality-of-life scores, alongside lower oxidative-stress markers; it had no control group.[23] A broader 2013 review lists acne among possible applications beyond weight loss.[24]

Reported effects include constipation, low-grade acidosis, raised blood lipids, and early lethargy that usually resolves within two weeks.[1] During the transition people also report headache, dizziness, insomnia and nausea, and breath may smell fruity from acetone.[2] A review in Atherosclerosis noted rapid weight loss and favorable biomarker changes alongside a substantial rise in LDL cholesterol that makes many physicians hesitant.[15] In children on the medical diet, lipids rise in up to 60 percent, and long-term risks include slowed growth, fractures and kidney stones in about 1 in 20.[1]

Case reports describe ketoacidosis on low-carbohydrate diets, and headache, bad breath and cramps are common. Wikipedia also lists case reports of thiamine-deficiency optic neuropathy and Wernicke's encephalopathy, malnutrition from restriction and difficulty reaching adequate fiber. Contraindications for the medical diet include pyruvate carboxylase deficiency, porphyria and fatty-acid oxidation disorders.[1] The American Medical Association, American Dietetic Association and American Heart Association have called the Atkins approach nutritionally unbalanced, and a 2004 lawsuit by a dieter who reported raised LDL and angioplasty was dismissed in 2007.[10]

Epilepsy trials found seizures reduced by more than 50 percent in about half of patients, and a 2018 Cochrane review of 11 randomized trials is described as finding about 38 percent of children on the diet with half or fewer seizures against 6 percent of controls.[1] For weight, a meta-analysis of eight randomized trials in overweight adults with type 2 diabetes found significant reductions in weight, waist circumference, HbA1c and triglycerides.[6] The Keto-Med crossover trial compared a ketogenic with a Mediterranean-style diet on glycated hemoglobin in prediabetes and type 2 diabetes.[25] A randomized trial in women with PCOS compared moderate-carbohydrate and ketogenic diets on body measures and hormones.[26] A 2025 randomized trial tested keto against time-restricted eating and alternate-day fasting.[7] A systematic review of dietary cholesterol and cardiovascular disease found heterogeneous, methodologically weak studies and drew no firm conclusions on cardiovascular risk.[27]

On looksmax.org, threads range from praise of keto and animal-based diets to critiques that carbohydrates are needed for muscle gain.[13] One poster shared an argument citing cardiology that LDL cholesterol is an independent risk factor, while others pushed back citing influencers who argue otherwise.[28] T Nation members describe keto as their chosen cutting method, and some use cyclical variants.[29][17] A Hacker News thread discussed large cohort studies that raised questions about low-carbohydrate diets.[30]

The carnivore diet, with nineteenth-century precursors such as James Salisbury's meat-and-hot-water regimen, spread through social media after 2018, when former orthopaedic surgeon Shawn Baker promoted it; Jordan Peterson and his daughter Mikhaila described following a beef-salt-water 'lion diet'; and in 2024 Paul Saladino popularised an animal-based variant that allows fruit, honey and raw dairy.[12] Wikipedia reports that nutrition scientists and the British Dietetic Association classify carnivore eating as a fad diet, citing micronutrient gaps, low fiber and raised LDL.[12]

The ketogenic diet is a medically supervised therapy for refractory epilepsy and has been studied for conditions including Alzheimer's disease, polycystic kidney disease and psychiatric illness, with trials such as KETO-ADPKD and a bipolar and schizophrenia pilot trial.[1] Wikipedia states that, as of 2022, there is no clinical evidence that the diet treats cancer.[1] Commercial keto foods and exogenous ketone products are sold as supplements and are outside this article's scope.

lore.intro: Keto is discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation mainly as a fat-loss tool, with disagreement over muscle gain, cholesterol and how far to go toward carnivore eating.[13][28][29]
